source_text: Quid de eo boni sentias, quem timorem fuisse apud eum, quam fidem credas quem corrigere nec metus potuit, quem persecutio ipsa non reformavit? Alta et erecta cervix nec quia cecidit inflexa est. Tumens animus et superbus nec quia victus est fractus est. Jacens stantibus et integris vulneratus miratur; et quod non statim Domini corpus inquinatis manibus accipiat, aut ore polluto Domini sanguinem bibat, sacerdotibus sacrilegus irascitur. Atque, o tuam nimiam, furiose, dementiam! Irasceris ei qui abs te avertere iram Dei nititur; ei minaris qui pro te Domini misericordiam deprecatur, qui vulnus tuum sentit quod ipse non sentis, qui pro te lacrymas fundit, quas forsitan ipse non fundis. Oneras adhuc crimen et cumulas; et cum sis ipse implacabilis ad antistites et sacerdotes Dei, putas circa te Dominum posse placari?
pass_a_gloss: What good do you think there was in him, in whom there was fear, what faith do you believe there was, which not even fear could correct, which not even persecution itself reformed? The neck, lofty and erect, was not bent even though it fell. The soul, swollen and proud, was not broken even though it was conquered. Lying among the standing and unharmed, he is wounded and marvels; and because he does not immediately receive the Lord's body with polluted hands, or drink the Lord's blood with a polluted mouth, he rages sacrilegiously against the priests. And, oh your excessive, furious, madness! You rage against him who strives to turn away God's anger from you; you threaten him who prays for the Lord's mercy for you, who feels your wound which you yourself do not feel, who pours out tears for you, which perhaps you yourself do not pour out. You still burden the crime and heap it up; and although you yourself are unyielding towards the bishops and priests of God, you think that the Lord can be placated concerning you?
pass_b_english: What good could you possibly think was in him—he who knew fear, yet whom not even fear could correct? What faith could you believe he had, when persecution itself failed to reform him? His neck, lofty and erect, refused to bend even when he fell. His soul, swollen with pride, refused to break even when he was conquered. Lying wounded among those who stand whole and unharmed, he marvels; and because he cannot immediately receive the Lord's body with polluted hands, or drink the Lord's blood with a polluted mouth, he rages sacrilegiously against the priests. Oh, your excessive, furious madness! You rage against the one who strives to turn God's anger away from you; you threaten the one who pleads for the Lord's mercy on your behalf, who feels your wound though you do not feel it yourself, who pours out tears for you that perhaps you yourself do not shed. You keep piling up the crime, heaping it higher; and when you yourself are unyielding toward the bishops and priests of God, do you really think the Lord can be placated toward you?

review.notes: Pass A and Pass B both accurately reflect the Latin text. Pass B provides a more idiomatic rendering of the rhetorical questions and the final clause, while maintaining the semantic integrity of the original. All clauses, including the descriptions of the neck and soul, are preserved.
